subject: biology-hl
about: Original practice questions written for NevaIB from the IB guide's syllabus understandings and the school's unit order. Not IB past-paper questions, not publisher material and not IB markschemes: the marking points are written for self-marking. Organisms, experiments and data in data-response items are invented for practice.

items.stem: Phospholipids form a bilayer in water because:
choices: They have hydrophilic heads and hydrophobic tails
They are entirely hydrophobic molecules
They form covalent bonds with the surrounding water molecules
Their tails are attracted to water molecules
items.note: Amphipathic molecules arrange with heads facing water on both sides and tails facing each other inside.

items.stem: Which molecule can cross a membrane by simple diffusion through the bilayer?
choices: Glucose
Sodium ions
Proteins
Oxygen
items.note: Small, non-polar molecules (O₂, CO₂) pass through the hydrophobic core. Ions and polar molecules like glucose need proteins; proteins need vesicles.

items.stem: Facilitated diffusion differs from active transport because facilitated diffusion:
choices: Moves substances against their gradient using energy from ATP hydrolysis
Needs no membrane proteins
Moves substances down their concentration gradient without ATP
Only moves water
items.note: Facilitated diffusion is passive, through channel or carrier proteins. Active transport uses pump proteins and ATP to move substances against the gradient.

items.stem: In the fluid mosaic model, "mosaic" refers to:
choices: Phospholipids that move freely sideways
Proteins scattered in the phospholipid bilayer
Cholesterol molecules wedged between the fatty acid tails
Carbohydrates forming a coat outside
items.note: "Fluid" = phospholipids and proteins move laterally; "mosaic" = the pattern of proteins embedded in the bilayer.

items.stem: Glycoproteins on the outer surface of a plasma membrane are involved mainly in:
choices: Active transport of ions
Cell recognition and cell adhesion
Increasing membrane fluidity in the cold
Synthesis of ATP
items.note: Carbohydrate chains act as markers (e.g. blood groups, self vs non-self) and help cells stick together.

items.stem: Phospholipids with more unsaturated fatty acid tails make a membrane:
choices: More fluid, because kinks stop tails packing closely
Less fluid, because double bonds are stronger
More rigid, because tails are straighter
Unchanged, because tails do not affect fluidity
items.note: Cis double bonds put kinks in tails, so they pack loosely. Organisms in cold environments increase unsaturation to stay fluid.

choices: Forms hydrophilic channels so ions can pass through the bilayer
Carries out active transport using ATP
Regulates fluidity, reducing it at higher temperatures
Acts as a receptor for hormones
items.note: Cholesterol sits between phospholipid tails and restrains movement, stabilising fluidity over a range of temperatures.

items.stem: The sodium–potassium pump moves ions in each cycle as follows:
choices: 2 Na⁺ out and 3 K⁺ in, using one ATP
3 Na⁺ in and 2 K⁺ out, using no ATP
1 Na⁺ out and 1 K⁺ in, using two ATP
3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in, using one ATP
items.note: Three sodium ions are pumped out and two potassium ions in, per ATP hydrolysed — this builds the resting potential gradient.

items.stem: Glucose is absorbed into intestinal cells against its concentration gradient by a sodium–glucose cotransporter. The energy for this comes directly from:
choices: ATP binding to the cotransporter protein
Diffusion of glucose down its own concentration gradient into the cell
Osmosis of water into the epithelial cell
The sodium concentration gradient made by the Na⁺/K⁺ pump
items.note: Indirect (secondary) active transport: Na⁺ moves down its gradient, carrying glucose with it. The pump using ATP maintains the Na⁺ gradient.

items.stem: A voltage-gated potassium channel opens when:
choices: The membrane potential changes to a particular value
Acetylcholine binds to a receptor site on the channel protein
ATP is hydrolysed by the channel
The concentration of K⁺ outside rises
items.note: Voltage-gated channels respond to membrane potential (e.g. during an action potential). The nicotinic acetylcholine receptor is a ligand-gated channel.

choices: Channel proteins that open wide enough to let large molecules through the membrane
Simple diffusion of water through aquaporins
The fluidity of the membrane, which allows vesicles to bud off and fuse
The rigidity of the membrane, which keeps vesicles in shape
items.note: Fluid membranes can pinch in (endocytosis) or fuse with vesicles (exocytosis); both use ATP.

items.stem: Explain how the structure of the phospholipid bilayer makes the membrane partially permeable.
markscheme: Hydrophobic core of fatty acid tails (1)
Prevents passage of ions and polar molecules (1)
Small non-polar molecules (and small amounts of water) can diffuse through (1)
Proteins are needed for other substances, giving selectivity (1)
items.tactic: Link structure → property → consequence, per marking point.

items.stem: Distinguish between channel proteins and pump proteins.
markscheme: Channel proteins allow passive movement (down a gradient); pumps move substances against a gradient (1)
Pumps need ATP/energy; channels do not (1)
Channels form a pore; pumps change shape to carry the substance (1)
items.tactic: Distinguish: pair each feature on the same line.

items.stem: Describe how the sodium–potassium pump works.
markscheme: Three Na⁺ bind to the pump from inside the cell (1)
ATP is hydrolysed and a phosphate attaches, so the pump changes shape and releases Na⁺ outside (1)
Two K⁺ bind from outside, causing the phosphate to be released (1)
The pump returns to its original shape and releases K⁺ inside (1)
items.tactic: Mechanisms: number each step and say what triggers the next.

items.stem:
(Invented data for practice.) Beetroot pieces were heated for 1 minute at different temperatures, then left in water. Red pigment leaking out was measured as light absorbance (invented data): 20 °C 0.05; 40 °C 0.08; 50 °C 0.22; 60 °C 0.61; 70 °C 0.95.
(a) Describe the effect of temperature on pigment leakage. (b) Explain the results in terms of membrane structure. (c) State two variables that must be controlled.
markscheme: (a) Little change from 20 to 40 °C (0.05 to 0.08), then a sharp rise to 0.95 at 70 °C (1)
(b) Higher temperature increases fluidity / phospholipids move more (1)
Membrane proteins denature above about 40–50 °C, leaving gaps (1)
(c) Two of: size/surface area of beetroot pieces; volume of water; time in water; beetroot rinsed before; same beetroot source (1)
items.tactic: Unfamiliar context: find the syllabus idea being tested, quote the data (with units) when you describe a trend, then explain it with that idea. One marking point per linked step.
